system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2154-07-15 21:22:00 to 2154-07-24 17:43:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of end-stage renal disease due to diabetic nephropathy, kidney transplant, peripheral vascular disease, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for chest pain in the setting of hypertensive urgency with systolic blood pressures up to 240 mmHg. He presented with substernal pressure radiating to the back and evidence of mild to moderate pulmonary edema on chest imaging. His troponin was minimally elevated but consistent with his baseline due to chronic kidney disease. He was treated with intravenous nitroglycerin to control blood pressure and IV furosemide for fluid overload, with improvement in symptoms and resolution of pulmonary congestion. A renal ultrasound ruled out renal artery stenosis, and transplant nephrology recommended outpatient evaluation for pheochromocytoma. His antihypertensive regimen was optimized with increased labetalol and discontinuation of nifedipine. He was discharged home on adjusted medications, with instructions to monitor weight and blood pressure, and to follow up for a sleep study, chem 7, and pheochromocytoma workup.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic chronic kidney disease

Mr. ___ is a ___ year old man with a history of HFpEF (LVEF 
69%), ESRD due to diabetic nephropathy s/p failed renal 
transplant in ___ and S/P repeat renal transplant in ___ with 
stage 4 CKD (baseline Cr recently 3.8-4), calciphylaxis, OSA 
(used O2 3 LPM at night), PAD s/p multiple bilateral 
revascularizations and left BKA presenting with dyspnea and 
hypertension.

Mr. ___ noticed on ___ afternoon that his home SBPs were in 
the 240s all day while he was checking it. He said that he 
usually checks his blood pressure 3 times a day with an 
automated arm blood pressure cuff. He says that he has been very 
compliant with his home antihypertensive medications. However, 
upon discussing the doses with him, he realizes that he may have 
been taking only 1 of the labetalol tablets as opposed to the 
usual two that he had been taking. He states that he got a 
recent prescription that was 200 mg as opposed to the previous 
300 mg tablets and therefore he was possibly taking only two 
tablets in the AM and evening as opposed to the 3 that he should 
be taking to make the total 600 mg dose AM and QHS. 

On ___ evening after his BP was elevated all day, he had 
wheeziness with his breathing and a tightness and pressure in 
his chest. He says that this has happened before and was similar 
each time. He had taken his medications. He also had some cough, 
with clear mucus, but no fevers or chills (T 98.2F). He did take 
his medications. He has been admitted multiple times previously 
for similar presentations due to poorly controlled hypertension.

He was admitted from ___ through ___ for 
hypertensive urgency with atypical chest pain. At that time, his 
systolic blood pressure ranged between 170-240, and this was 
similarly associated with this chest tightness. His chest 
discomfort was thought to be secondary to subendocardial 
ischemia from strain with the elevated afterload. His baseline 
troponins are thought do be around 0.18 given his ESRD. On that 
hospitalization, he required a nitroglycerin drip before being 
able to be controlled on his home blood pressure regimen. 
Notably a renal ultrasound was negative for evidence of renal 
artery stenosis on admission. There was a recommendation to do a 
pheochromocytoma work-up as an outpatient. He also required 
diuresis with furosemide IV before being placed back in his home 
regimen.

In the ED, initial vital signs were notable for: Temp 98.6 HR 72 
BP 244/109 RR 18 SaO2 96% on O2 2 LPM via NC. Exam notable for a 
right-sided port, regular rhythm, left-sided crackles, left BKA, 
no peripheral edema. Labs were notable for WBC 6.6 Hgb 8.5 Plt 
134 INR: 1.2 Na 141 K 3.4 Cl 100 HC03 23 BUN 71 Cr. 4.7 Trop-T 
0.17 -> 0.20 -> 0.18, NT-Pro-BNP: 34718. UA: protein 300, Ketone 
neg, Bacteria few. Renal US showed abnormal intrarenal waveforms 
demonstrating absence of antegrade diastolic flow corresponding 
with a resistive index of 1.0. Patient was given nitroglycerin 
0.3 mg sl X 2, pravastatin 40 mg, labetolol 600+400+600 mg po, 
nifedpine 90 mg po, furosemide 60 mg IV, tacrolimus 0.5+4.5 mg, 
prednisone 3 mg, insulin 2+2+4 units, Creon 12 3 cap. Renal felt 
there was no urgent indication for hemodialysis and advised 
re-dosing furosemide to maintain urine output of 100-125 cc/hr 
with goal negative 2 L over 24 hours. They also recommended 
titrating down TNG infusion to slowly reduce BP but not less 
than SBP of 160 on the day of admission. Vital signs on 
transfer: Temp 98.3 HR 71 BP 168/71 RR 18 O2 sat 98% on RA.

above history. He said that overall his breathing was much 
improved and he was not as wheezy. He stated that he continued 
to have the chest discomfort located at the xiphoid area of his 
abdomen/chest. He did not feel that it radiated into his arms or 
spreads to his back. He said that overall it was much more 
tolerable and he also thought that there may be a component of 
gastritis to his chest tightness. Interestingly he described 
this as if there is a baseball or something taking up space in 
the epigastric/xiphoid area.

chills, lower extremity edema, weight gain, nausea, vomiting,

Mr. ___ is a ___ man with a history of ESRD secondary

Patient's blood pressure was very difficult to control but he 
was discharged on a stable regimen.

ACTIVE ISSUES: 
# Severe asymptomatic hypertension, chest pain: Patient with 
acute onset shortness of breath, wheezing and variable 
descriptions of chest tightness in setting of severe 
hypertension with SBP in 240s. This likely led to a pulmonary 
hypertensive state and increased wall stretch and stress leading 
to possible subendocardial ischemia. Troponin-T elevated but at 
baseline in setting of ESRD. There was no rise and fall in 
troponin-T to suggest an acute myonecrotic event. Etiology of 
his recurrent hypertensive episodes and frequent 
hospitalizations remains unclear. Urine metanepherines were low. 
Transplant renal ultrasound was without obvious inflow artery 
stenosis. Labile blood pressures intermittently requiring 
nitroglycerin drip as well as midodrine because he became 
symptomatic with occasional systolic blood pressure <130 mmHg. 
Nifedipine was discontinued and he was discharged on amlodipine 
10 mg, doxazosin 16 mg, labetalol 800 mg TID, and hydralazine 
100 mg PO TID.

# Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting: Patient with severe, 
acute-onset epigastric pain with benign abdominal exam. Given 
vascular history, initial thoughts that this was hypo-perfusion 
related mesenteric infarct in setting of relative hypotension. 
Lactate and abdominal X ray were normal without obstructive 
pattern. This resolved prior to discharge with better blood 
pressure control. 

# Pulmonary edema, HFpEF: Patient with heart failure preserved 
ejection fraction and acute onset pulmonary edema in the setting 
of hypertensive urgency. Overall on exam he appeared to be 
euvolemic and his weight per the report from home and from his 
vitals did not suggest a volume overloaded state. He received 
furosemide IV in the ED but he was transitioned to his home 
torsemide shortly after admission. Heart failure therapy was 
directed at better control of his systolic blood pressure.

# Thrombocytopenia (RESOLVED): Patient with acute onset from 
thrombocytopenia with platelets in the 130s from previous 
170-190 baseline. His platelets were monitored and normalized 
prior to discharge.

continued on a reduced dose of his home glargine 13 units a.m at 
8 units.

# Peripheral arterial disease: Patient with prior left leg 
dorsalis pedis bypass with resultant left below the knee 
amputation setting of infection. He uses a prosthetic leg. He 
was continued on aspirin 81 mg PO daily and his pravastatin was 
changed to atorvastatin 40 mg PO qhs.

# ESRD s/p ___ renal transplant ___: ESRD secondary to diabetic 
nephropathy (s/p failed LRRT in ___ now with a functioning DDRT 
implanted in ___. Baseline Cr ___. He continued daily 
prednisone 3 mg daily as well as tacrolimus increased to 5 mg 
BID. He will follow-up with transplant nephrology as outpatient. 
He does not need to continue taking his leflunomide.

# Pancreatic insufficiency: Patient has a history of chronic 
epigastric pain and a history of pancreatic insufficiency. He 
was continued on his home Creon 3 times daily with meals

# Chronic anemia: Patient with baseline anemia hemoglobin 
baseline between 7.9-8.5.
Normocytic and likely related to CKD.

# OSA: Patient was unable to use CPAP machine as an outpatient 
and requires repeat sleep study. Baseline use of O2 3 LPM via NC 
at night.

renal cysts. Will repeat US in ___ year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in because of high blood pressure and trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. My blood pressure was in the 240s all day. I check it three times daily. I’ve had this before—tight chest, wheezing. I thought it was just another flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were given some nitroglycerin in the ER and your BP came down to 168. We’re going to monitor you closely. Did you take your usual blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I did, but… I got a new prescription. The labetalol tablets are 200 mg now instead of 300 mg. I might have only taken two instead of three in the morning and evening. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could definitely explain it. Taking less than your prescribed dose, even unintentionally, can cause your pressure to spike. We’ll adjust your meds carefully here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been admitted like this before. Always high BP, chest tightness. They said it might be strain on the heart. Is that what’s happening again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. When your blood pressure is very high, your heart has to work harder. That can cause chest discomfort and even mild fluid buildup in the lungs, which we see on your chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray showed fluid? But I didn’t feel that swollen. No leg swelling or weight gain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with your type of heart failure—preserved ejection fraction. You can have pulmonary edema without obvious swelling. We gave you IV furosemide in the ER to help clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my troponin was 0.17—does that mean a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. With your kidney disease, your baseline troponin is higher. It didn’t rise and fall, so it’s likely chronic. No sign of a new heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But why do my BPs keep spiking like this? I’ve been trying to stay on top of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. We checked your renin and aldosterone levels. Your renin is low, aldosterone is low—so it’s not a hormonal tumor like pheochromocytoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Could be your medications aren’t strong enough, or there’s resistance due to your kidney transplant and vascular disease. We’re adjusting your regimen to be more effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had that weird pain in my upper belly—like a baseball was stuck there. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were concerned it could be poor blood flow to the gut, given your vascular history. But your lactate and abdominal X-ray were normal, so it’s likely related to the blood pressure swings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better now that my BP is down. Should I still worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It resolved with treatment, so we don’t think it’s serious. But we’ll keep monitoring. Your platelets were also a bit low when you came in—down from your usual. We’re watching that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was mild, and they’re already improving. Could be from your medications or chronic condition. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your platelets are trending back up, and your breathing is better. We’re switching you from IV furosemide to your home torsemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my blood pressure meds? Are we changing those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re stopping nifedipine and starting amlodipine, which may work better for you. We’re also increasing labetalol and adding hydralazine to help stabilize your pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hydralazine? I’ve never taken that before. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can cause headaches or low BP. If your systolic drops below 130 and you feel dizzy, stop the hydralazine and call your doctor. But keep taking the labetalol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my insulin? I noticed they reduced it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered your glargine from 13 to 8 units to avoid low blood sugar. Monitor your sugars at home and increase slowly if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. What about my transplant kidney? I remember the ultrasound showed something odd.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed normal structure, but the blood flow in the small arteries has high resistance—resistive index of 1.0. It’s not new, and your main artery is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Could it affect my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign of chronic changes, likely from high BP and diabetes. We’re increasing your tacrolimus to 5 mg twice daily to protect the transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I don’t need leflunomide anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, transplant team says you can stop it. We’ll follow up with them as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray was clear—no blockage. The pain seems linked to your BP. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. No belly pain, no chest tightness. Breathing is easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your oxygen levels are normal, and lungs are clear. We’re continuing your new BP meds and will watch for stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been more stable—around 170s systolic. We’re hopeful this new combination is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel steady. But will I keep having these episodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re trying to prevent that. If BPs stay high, your doctor might add a thiazide diuretic like chlorthalidone. The key is consistency with meds and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful with the doses. What about my sleep apnea? I still can’t use the CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend a repeat sleep study. You’re on oxygen at night, but better airflow could help your BP control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Hemoglobin is stable, creatinine is 4.7—same as baseline. Platelets are back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any update on the kidney mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI showed small complex cysts. You’ll need a repeat ultrasound in a year to monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow. Your BP is stable, symptoms are gone, and labs are acceptable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take amlodipine, doxazosin at night, hydralazine three times a day, and labetalol three times daily. Plus your usual Creon, aspirin, and transplant meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 8 units glargine in the morning. Watch your sugars and increase if they’re high. Check your creatinine in a week and tacrolimus levels as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if my BP drops too low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If systolic is under 130 and you feel dizzy, stop the hydralazine. Keep taking the others and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your physical exam is clear. Lungs are clear, no swelling, heart rhythm normal. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for helping me get stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge today. We’ll go over your instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications as listed. Attend your follow-ups: sleep study, nephrology, and lab work. Check tacrolimus levels on the date specified.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel chest tightness again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your BP. If it’s over 180, take your usual meds and rest. If it doesn’t improve or you feel worse, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks, Doctor. I’ll be more careful with my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re being discharged home today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready. Thank you again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay on your meds, monitor your BP, and call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, end-stage renal disease with two kidney transplants, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, peripheral arterial disease with left below-knee amputation, and obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for hypertensive urgency with systolic blood pressures reaching 244 mmHg, associated with chest tightness and mild pulmonary edema. The episode was partly attributed to unintentional underdosing of labetalol due to a change in tablet strength. He also experienced transient epigastric pain concerning for mesenteric ischemia, though workup was negative. His blood pressure was stabilized with IV nitroglycerin initially, followed by transition to oral amlodipine, doxazosin, hydralazine, and increased labetalol, while nifedipine was discontinued. He received IV furosemide for pulmonary congestion and was transitioned back to home torsemide. His platelet count, which dipped during admission, normalized. He was discharged home on an adjusted antihypertensive regimen with close follow-up for transplant care, sleep apnea reassessment, and monitoring of kidney mass and medication levels.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic (congestive) heart failure
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic nephropathy
Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease
Peripheral artery disease with left below knee amputation
